item.title: Xi calls for balancing nation's development, security
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
Xi calls for balancing nation's development, security President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to advance the Peaceful China Initiative to a higher level to ensure steady and sustained progress in Chinese modernization. Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in his recent instruction on the initiative. His instruction was conveyed at a working conference on the initiative held on Monday in Beijing. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, China has made significant progress in building a safe country, further consolidating a sound environment in which people live and work in peace and society remains stable and orderly, Xi said, adding that China has become one of the safest countries in the world. On the new journey, China should firmly implement a holistic approach to national security and uphold and strengthen the Party's overall leadership in this area, Xi said. He stressed better coordinating development and security, combining punishment with prevention and addressing both the symptoms and root causes of problems. He also called for strengthening legal support and leveraging technology to enhance the construction of the national security system and capabilities, and guarding against and defusing various risks. According to the CPC Central Committee's Commission for Political and Legal Affairs, China recorded its lowest number of criminal and homicide cases this century in 2025, while the public's satisfaction rate regarding safety reached 98.23 percent, remaining above 98 percent for a sixth consecutive year. The downward trend of such cases continued in the first half of the year, with criminal cases falling 16.5 percent year-on-year, homicide cases down 11.4 percent, and gun-related cases dropping 53.3 percent. Authorities have continued regular operations against organized crime and intensified efforts to combat telecommunications and online fraud, while working to prevent risks in areas including finance, real estate and labor relations. Beyond combating crime, grassroots mechanisms for resolving disputes have also been expanded. About 9.76 million disputes were resolved through such mechanisms in 2025 and another 7.13 million in the first half of this year. The total number of petitions in 2025 fell to its lowest level this century, according to the commission. The Peaceful China Initiative will place greater emphasis on risk monitoring and early warning, prevention-oriented public security governance, and the resolution of disputes at the grassroots level, the meeting said. Efforts will also be intensified to combat serious violent crimes, gun — and explosives-related offenses, human trafficking and telecom fraud, while grassroots disputes will be addressed at an early stage to prevent them from escalating into serious criminal cases.

item.title: Smartphone 'detox' a refresh for peace of mind
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
Smartphone 'detox' a refresh for peace of mind Reduced screen time frees users from shackles of work, constant scrolling What can a person do in 134 days without a smartphone or mobile internet? For Yang Hao, the answer was "quite a lot". He crossed 24 provincial-level regions and traveled through 68 cities and counties. He read nearly 40 books, recorded about two terabytes of footage and wrote roughly 220,000 Chinese characters, much of it while on the road. Before he embarked on the journey, another measure had been bothering him: six hours and 57 minutes. That was the average amount of time Yang spent on his phone every day in a week. There was nothing especially unusual about what filled those hours. He worked, answered messages on WeChat and browsed social media. Often, he said, he picked up the phone without quite knowing why. The habit had begun to trouble him during the pandemic, when more of everyday life seemed to migrate onto screens. "I started wondering: If I reject the phone and this whole system, can I still live normally?" Yang said. Natural rhythm In late 2023, Yang, who was pursuing a doctorate in the United Kingdom, returned to China and decided to find out. He switched off his smartphone and computer and left them behind. Setting out from his hometown of Taiyuan, Shanxi province, he spent the next 134 days without apps providing mobile payments, navigation, ride-hailing, online hotel bookings or social media. Yang picked a general direction, slung a backpack over his shoulders and set off armed with only a map. Instead of following itineraries recommended on social media platforms, he decided he would arrive somewhere by train, randomly board a local bus and see where it took him. If something along the way caught his eye, he got off. In each new city, he usually started at a museum to get a sense of the place, then visited a local bookstore, looking for clues to places that might interest him. At other times, conversations with local people determined where he went next. Yang's journey gradually acquired its own rhythm. He became fond of slower, conventional trains. Through the window, he said, "the landscape drifted past like scenes from a film". Without a phone, he could not book tickets in advance, so he was often forced to wait. Sometimes that meant spending two or three hours in a rundown waiting room in a county town before the next train or bus arrived. At first, those intervals made him uneasy. There was no feed to refresh in a waiting room, no message to check five minutes before boarding, no short video to make a delay disappear. So he read. He made notes, watched passengers and looked through windows. Sometimes he simply sat. "Of all the things I experienced, perhaps the most important was learning how to pass time in a more interesting way," Yang wrote in his notes. "How to wait is an art. Before, the thing I held for the longest every day was my phone. Now it is a book," he said. What he had not expected, however, was that living without a phone made him look suspicious to some people. At a bus station in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Yang was trying to buy a ticket to Ningcheng county when a station worker suggested that he check something on his phone. Yang told her he did not use one. The woman stared at him. If he carried no phone, she said aloud, perhaps there was a reason he did not want people to know where he was. Others nearby began listening. Eventually, according to Yang's account in his book Guanji, which he refers to in English as Disconnected: A Happy Excursion Against the Digital Leviathan, the woman reached a conclusion. "You must be a spy," she said. Yang found the scene funny. He also found it revealing. He had removed only one ordinary object from his life, yet to the people around him, going without it seemed almost as unnatural as missing a part of his body. A smartphone, he was beginning to realize, had become more than something one carried. Not carrying one could make a person appear out of place. "The whole social system seems to assume that everyone is online all the time," Yang said. "People expect to be able to find you, and they expect you to respond." Disconnect to reconnect A smartphone can neatly fill those minutes that seem empty — waiting in a line, standing on a train platform, or killing time before a friend arrives. Social media makes those gaps easy to fill. There is always another video, photograph, opinion or notification waiting beneath the last one. DataReportal's Digital 2026 report found that adults spend an average of 18 hours and 36 minutes a week on social networks and video feeds. Among women aged 16 to 24, the figure rises to 25 hours and 45 minutes. Xu Yaqian, a self-employed designer, tried something much smaller than Yang's experiment that was no less revealing. "During the first boom in short videos a few years ago, there were times when I scrolled until almost dawn," Xu said. "It felt as if the phone had been enchanted and grown into my hand. I was exhausted, anxious and blaming myself, but I still wouldn't put it down." Xu felt his attention becoming increasingly fragmented. He could barely remain focused for a few minutes before reaching automatically for the phone, opening a social-media app, and then scrolling. "I would go online to look up one specific piece of information," he said, "and suddenly realize I was watching a Xiaohongshu creator explain how she decorated her bedroom." The problem is not confined to China. Most adults in the United States age under 30 said their phone is the first and last thing they look at every day, according to a recent YouGov poll. Nearly 40 percent sleep with it next to them. Even internet slang captures the unease: compulsive scrolling has given rise to terms such as "doomscrolling" and "brain rot". Xu began setting limits on screen time, replacing scrolling with films and books, spending more time outdoors and seeking face-to-face interaction. After about half a year of trying, he reached his goal this year, reducing his daily screen time from five or six hours to one or two. The desire to step away is spreading, and a business has grown around it. One product, called Brick, uses a small device to block selected apps and websites. Regaining access requires users to tap their phone against the device again, adding a physical obstacle between impulse and action. On Taobao, Chinese consumers can buy an even more literal version. Search for "smartphone detox" and rows of time-restricted phone lockboxes appear. A phone is placed inside the box until the timer expires. Some listings showed thousands of people had paid for such products. Meanwhile, phone-free gatherings have appeared in cities including Amsterdam and London, where participants put away their devices to read, draw, play games or talk to strangers. Rise of 'slow media' The turn away from constant connectivity goes beyond simply putting phones aside. In Slow Media: Why Slow Is Satisfying, Sustainable, and Smart, media scholar Jennifer Rauch examines a renewed attraction to books, handwritten letters, vinyl records, film photography and other forms of media that demand more time and attention. Rather than rejecting technology altogether, the idea is to reclaim some choice over the pace at which media enters everyday life. Yang's journey reflected this idea. During his 134 days offline, books replaced his phone, while physical maps, slow trains and unplanned encounters did the job of digital-assisted travel. Slower forms of media, he said, can leave more room for "thinking and understanding". But choosing to slow down is not easy for everyone. Hu Yong, a professor at Peking University's School of Journalism and Communication, has argued that excessive phone use cannot simply come down to a matter of willpower. When work, life and entertainment all take place on the same device, getting rid of it completely can be unrealistic. Hu has also warned against shifting all responsibility onto users when hardware and apps themselves are designed to keep people engaged. Zhang Ran, 28, who works in foreign trade in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, said: "I can't really get away from my phone. From the moment I open my eyes, my work is already running across my phone and computer." Even at the gym, she checks her phone to see whether a client or supervisor needs her. Her workday usually starts at 9 am and can sometimes stretch past 10 pm. "I always feel as if very little of the day actually belonged to me," Zhang said. To compensate, she said she scrolls to relieve her stress. A clip from a television program she has already watched. Then another. Sometimes it is two or three in the morning before she stops. Zhang has tried to break the cycle. Once, she turned off her phone for an entire Saturday and spent much of the day reading. "Time felt both fast and slow," Zhang said. "It felt like I had recovered a familiarity with time that I'd lost." But as her work became busier in recent months, those phone-free Saturdays disappeared. "Sometimes I still have to answer work messages on weekends," she said. "I feel like I'm always online." Call of duty Zhang's dilemma represents what some believe is now a labor issue. Shanghai labor law expert Lu Jingbo has argued that mobile and remote work are increasingly blurring the boundary between work and rest, making it more difficult for workers to truly disconnect outside working hours. For Zhang, turning off Xiaohongshu is one thing, but ignoring a client is another. "If a job that requires me to stay attached to my phone keeps making me feel worse," she said, "I may quit and rest for a while, and try to find my focus again." After his journey, Yang collated the observations in his notes into a manuscript and approached several publishers. They turned him down. Ironically, the reversal in his literary fortune came from the very thing he had spent months trying to escape. A media report about his experiment began circulating online. It drew traffic and attention. Publishers began contacting him — including some that he had approached before, he said. "I tried to escape the virtual network woven by the internet and traffic," he said. "I didn't expect that traffic to be what brought the publishers back to me." Yang, who has since completed his PhD in contemporary art at Lancaster University and now teaches cross-media art at Beijing Institute of Fashion Technology, called the episode "particularly ironic". "It reflects how society works now," he said. "It is very difficult to escape the logic of the internet." He also acknowledges that modern life cannot simply be separated from the internet. The journey did not make him reject the smartphone. It changed the boundaries he wanted to draw around it. "When I'm working, reading or writing, I switch it off for a while," Yang said. "I still have to live by the rules of this society," he said. "But I also want to keep some independence for myself."

item.title: 'Chinese vintage' from a time gone by finds favor once again
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
When Edward Hugh Fraser, 45, was leaving Beijing to return to the United Kingdom, he wanted to take home a souvenir. Instead of choosing a box of tea or a fine silk scarf, he picked out a vintage-looking tin of clam oil — a petroleum jelly-like skin product known as "Chinese Vaseline" that was a familiar household item in China back in the 1960s and remains in production today. "It's hardly your typical tourist souvenir," Fraser said, adding that it allowed him to bring back a slice of local Chinese life. The clam oil that Fraser found was tucked away in Dafang Department Store, an old Beijing shop that retains the feel of a State-run shop from decades past. It was there that Fraser encountered everyday objects he had never imagined would still have a place in modern Beijing. On the shelves, he noticed white-and-red enamel basins and mugs. A sales assistant told him that such enamelware was commonly given as wedding gifts in China in the 1970s and 1980s. Nearby, a foot-pedal sewing machine from around the same era was still in use. Fraser noticed that customers still came to have quilts made for children who were heading back to boarding school. "What touched me most is that these vintage objects have preserved a way of life from the past, and they remain available to ordinary citizens today," he said. For Italian architect Fabrizio Gurrado, these relics of everyday life offer something else: a way for Chinese nostalgia and Western aesthetics to meet. Near the landmark Drum Tower in Beijing, Gurrado has transformed several enamel basins into pendant lamps hanging from the ceiling of an Italian restaurant. Against the restaurant's European-style interior, these distinctly Chinese objects do not feel out of place, Gurrado said, adding that their age is precisely part of their appeal. "The chipped edges, the faded colors, the typography — they carry a kind of imperfect elegance that fits very well into modern spaces," he said. But Gurrado's connection to these items goes beyond design. Having grown up in southern Italy in the 1970s and 1980s, he remembers similar enamelware in family homes. Picking up an old Chinese enamel mug can unexpectedly take him back to his childhood and evoke memories of his parents. "I see stories of family meals, of communal living, of thrift and care in them," he said. Such familiarity gives vintage items a resonance that can cross cultures: An everyday object from another country can evoke memories of home. That appeal is also traveling far beyond physical shops and interiors. On social media, Chinese retro goods and lifestyles have been finding audiences overseas, particularly among younger users. For example, traditional Chinese cloth shoes with "thousand-layer" soles went viral on TikTok. Some online users dubbed them the "Air Jordans of the BC era", drawing attention to the enduring craftsmanship behind the traditional footwear. Retro reimagined For many overseas observers, Chinese vintage may offer a glimpse into an unfamiliar past. For young Chinese, however, many of these objects are not exotic curiosities, but reminders of things once found in the homes of their parents and grandparents. That nostalgia is now inspiring them to reinterpret this heritage in contemporary ways. Chinese content creator Hu Yu, who grew up in the 1980s, has documented that disappearing material world through short videos. In one series, he visits surviving State-owned department stores, filming the goods still found inside. The videos have attracted viewers who use the comment sections to reminisce about similar items from their own childhoods. "It really surprised me," Hu said. For younger creators, old everyday objects also offer a distinctive visual language to work with. Their bold colors, simple forms and recognizable motifs can easily be recast in modern designs. Guo Minjie, 21, is a pattern designer for fuse beads, a craft popular among young Chinese enthusiasts. Rather than focusing only on familiar anime characters or pet motifs, she designed a series based on old Chinese household items such as sewing machines, bicycles, enamel basins and tin frog toys. When she posted the patterns in a fan group with more than 10,000 members, the designs quickly caught on. More than 2,000 people signed up for the series, with fans sharing their finished pieces and asking her to create more. "Real retro objects will eventually wear out, but creativity ensures that the family bonds and the evolving memories of the times behind them live on," Guo said.

item.title: AI boom boosts industrial profit growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
AI boom boosts industrial profit growth Electronics sector saw January to August profits surge 110% year-on-year China's industrial profits sustained double-digit growth in the first eight months of the year, as the global artificial intelligence boom bolstered earnings expansion and underscored the increasing contribution of new growth drivers, officials and experts said. However, monthly profit growth slowed for a fourth straight month in August, with gains still concentrated among upstream resource producers and high-tech manufacturers, strengthening the case for more forceful measures to boost domestic demand and smooth the transition from traditional to new growth drivers, they added. Their comments came as fresh data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed that profits at major industrial enterprises reached 5.27 trillion yuan ($785.23 billion) in the January to August period, up 15.7 percent year-on-year. Growth remained strong, although it eased from 17.6 percent in the first seven months. The electronics sector was a key driver of the increase, with profits surging 110 percent year-on-year and its contribution to overall industrial profit growth reaching 62 percent, the bureau noted. Yu Weining, chief statistician at the bureau's industrial statistics department, attributed this rapid growth to the wider application of new technologies such as AI, which boosted demand in related fields. "For instance, new energy vehicles, the internet of things and computing centers are driving up demand for chips," Yu said, noting that profits at makers of optoelectronic devices and discrete semiconductors rose 72 percent and 51.8 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, new growth drivers also played a central role as profits at major high-tech manufacturers jumped 54.7 percent year-on-year in the first eight months, outpacing overall industrial profit growth by 39 percentage points, NBS data showed. Highlighting the contribution of new growth drivers, Chen Mengyun, a macroeconomic analyst at Shenyin &Wanguo Futures, said electronics and other high-tech industries are likely to continue providing a strong boost to profit growth in the near term. However, the benefits have yet to spread widely to traditional industries, Chen said, adding that the persistent divergence in performance across sectors points to lingering weakness in end demand. Profit growth at major industrial enterprises eased to 4.2 percent year-on-year in August from 11.2 percent in July, extending the slowdown to a fourth consecutive month, NBS data showed. Echoing Chen's view, Ming Ming, chief economist at CITIC Securities, said strong profit growth among upstream resource producers and technology firms contrasted with continued pressure on many midstream and downstream industries. Automakers and producers of alcoholic beverages, food and pharmaceuticals continued to face pressure, he said. To put profit growth on a firmer footing, analysts called for stronger countercyclical policy support and closer coordination among fiscal, financial and industrial policies. Yan Xiang, a researcher at the research institute of China Chengxin International Credit Rating, urged faster implementation of existing measures, particularly efforts to translate funding from local government special-purpose bonds, special treasury bonds and policy-based financial instruments into concrete progress on projects. "Greater emphasis should be placed on boosting household consumption and improving business expectations," Yan said, calling for measures to stabilize employment, raise incomes, expand services consumption and reduce companies' financing and operating costs to encourage spending and investment. Looking ahead, industrial earnings remain well supported, although profit growth may face short-term pressure before stabilizing in the fourth quarter, said Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank. Wen said the high comparison base from last September would continue to weigh on year-on-year growth, with that pressure expected to ease markedly in the fourth quarter.

item.title: Innovation drives agri-growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
Innovation drives agri-growth Better seeds, smarter processing and new market links boost rural industries A winter cabbage variety that reduces reliance on imported seeds, drones that carry oranges down steep hillsides and a rice mill that cuts grain breakage are tackling different problems in Hubei province's agricultural industries. Across Hubei, research and new equipment are being connected with cultivation, processing and markets. The changes reach beyond improving harvests: they help growers overcome transport constraints, help processors reduce waste and make fuller use of raw materials, and help villages develop new sources of income. Wang Dongmei, an official with the provincial department of science and technology, said Hubei has prioritized scientific and technological innovation in its economic, social and agricultural development. Taking advantage of its strength in education, research and agriculture, the province is aligning agricultural research with industry needs and putting more research findings into practical use to support the development of modern agriculture, Wang said. According to local statistics, the added value of Hubei's primary industry reached 538.07 billion yuan ($80.13 billion) in 2025, up 3.5 percent year-on-year. Better seeds In Jiayu county, Xianning, efforts to strengthen the cabbage industry began with the seed. The county grows about 180,000 mu (12,000 hectares) of cabbage, producing 720,000 metric tons a year. But growers had long depended heavily on imported seeds, whose high prices and uncertain supplies made it harder to control production costs, said Qiu Zhengming, chief scientist with the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences. In 2008, Jiayu began working with a team led by Fang Zhiyuan of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences to develop varieties suited to local conditions. After a decade of research, Zhonggan 1305, developed for winter cultivation, was introduced in 2018. It now covers nearly 100,000 mu, accounting for about 70 percent of the county's winter cabbage area. Improvements extend beyond breeding in the county. At a vegetable science and technology demonstration park, sensors monitor temperature, humidity and pest activity. A digital platform helps standardize production from raising seedlings to harvesting, while QR codes trace vegetables to individual plots. Technology should keep vegetables affordable for consumers while allowing growers to make a profit, Qiu said. Ma Jiliang, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Economics and Development of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said Jiayu shows how scientific research can support local industries. Building a regional vegetable brand with a geographical indication depends on science and technology, Ma said, adding that varieties with independent intellectual property rights are key to the industry's competitiveness.

item.title: Cross-Strait trade defies political friction
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
Cross-Strait trade defies political friction Mainland welcomes back pomelos from Taiwan as economic exchanges soar Editor's note: The Taiwan question is a key focus for China and the international community. China Daily is publishing a series of reports to track hot Taiwan-related topics and address disinformation from the Democratic Progressive Party administration. Despite the repeated smearing of the Chinese mainland's economic goodwill by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities, the mainland continues to promote cross-Strait trade and investment, bringing Taiwan's Wendan pomelos — a seasonal delicacy from Taiwan fruit growers — into mainland households this holiday season. On Sept 22, ahead of the Mid-Autumn and National Day holidays, an event featuring over a dozen booths in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, brought together people from both sides of the Taiwan Strait to taste the pomelos from Taiwan — famous for their thin skins, intense sweetness, juicy flesh and delicate fragrance. Hsu Fu-hsien, president of the Taiwan Merchant Association in Shenzhen, said that preferential policies from the Chinese mainland side have allowed premium fruits from Taiwan to arrive fresh via direct sales. In 2022, the General Administration of Customs suspended imports of Taiwan citrus fruits, including pomelos, to prevent the entry of harmful pests and excessive pesticide residues. Thanks to the active efforts of local authorities and farmers in Taiwan counties including Hualien, pest-control and quality rectifications were implemented. As a result, the mainland resumed imports from qualified, registered orchards and packaging plants in 2024, further expanding the market entry in August. "A tiny pomelo is a miniature of cross-Strait economic exchange, and a testament to the shared hearts of the people," Hsu said. Sharing this sentiment, Roy Wang, a Taiwan businessman who has worked in Shenzhen for nine years, said, "Eating pomelos from my hometown brings a true taste of home, and I hope people here in Shenzhen can enjoy this flavor." This improved market access stems from solid policy support. Following 10 exchange-promoting measures released by the mainland on April 12, joint cross-Strait efforts based on the 1992 Consensus and opposition to "Taiwan independence" separatism have widened the mainland market for Taiwan's agricultural and fishery products. Consequently, multiple Taiwan pomelo orchards, packing plants and food enterprises have registered on the mainland. Backed by fast customs clearance and efficient logistics, the fruit has debuted at several mainland exhibitions and is being sold in supermarkets and on e-commerce platforms. This progress was reflected in June at the Straits Forum, a major annual cross-Strait exchange event held in Xiamen, Fujian province, where mainland buyers signed procurement agreements with Taiwan enterprises and associations, covering products such as pineapple custard apples and tea. According to Taiwan's agricultural authorities, while the island's shipments to the United States and Japan fell in the first half of this year, its agricultural exports to the mainland rose 11.3 percent. Tang Hua, an associate professor of cross-Strait relations at Xiamen University, said the mainland is the closest, largest and most stable market for Taiwan's agricultural products. Its short distance ensures fast shipping, while a vast consumer market provides stable, predictable sales channels, she said. Extensive policy support covering land, financing, sales, branding and logistics greatly reduces operational costs and expands market channels for Taiwan's farmers and small businesses, she said. Attending the pomelo promotion event in Shenzhen, Peng Qing'en, deputy director of the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said that both sides share close geographical, kinship and cultural ties, and the mainland remains a vital market for Taiwan agricultural enterprises to expand. As the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) progresses, industrial upgrading and domestic market expansion will continue to release development dividends, Peng said, welcoming more Taiwan businesses to seize the opportunities and integrate into the mainland market.

item.title: Commemorating Confucius holds modern meaning
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
The words of The Analects of Confucius rose into the autumn air, set to music at the Confucius Temple in Qufu, a county-level city in Jining, Shandong province, on Monday, as people stepped forward with flower baskets and bowed during a ceremony, which was part of a ritual that has continued in various forms for centuries in the hometown of the philosopher who lived more than 2,500 years ago. "It's very interesting, lively," said Jonah Dunch, a Canadian graduate student studying Chinese philosophy at Peking University in Beijing, who attended the 2026 Memorial Ceremony for Confucius. He was visiting Qufu for the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations, and said that the ceremony offered a glimpse into how Confucian traditions are being carried into the present. "You could see an interesting mix of ancient practices and texts, and modern things as well," Dunch said, adding that the experience gave him a sense of the influence Confucius continues to have in Chinese culture. "I can see that Chinese people respect Confucius," he said. This year marks the 2,577th anniversary of the birth of Confucius, an influential educator and philosopher whose teachings became the foundation of Confucianism, shaping Chinese society and thought for generations. He advocated teaching students regardless of their social background. The tradition of commemorating Confucius began in 478 BC, a year after his death, and has evolved to feature ancient music, ceremonial dances and traditional rituals. The gathering was part of this year's China International Confucius Cultural Festival, which is themed "For a World of Shared Peace and Harmony with Benevolence and Ancient Rituals". The festival drew about 300 participants from 44 countries and regions, including foreign dignitaries, diplomats, UNESCO Confucius Prize laureates, overseas travel agents and young Sinologists. The festival runs through Oct 7, taking Confucian culture to the world through study tours, bringing it into everyday life through temple fairs, promoting the reading of Confucian classics worldwide, and following Confucius' legacy along the Grand Canal. Wang Jiayi, vice-minister of education, highlighted Confucius' longstanding influence as an educator, citing principles including "education for all without discrimination", "teaching according to aptitude" and "learning with constant practice". Wang said that these ideas continue to have relevance today. He also referred to the UNESCO Confucius Prize for Literacy, established in 2005 with funding from Shandong. Over the past two decades, the prize has recognized dozens of literacy initiatives. This year's recipients from Lebanon, Mexico and Thailand have worked with out-of-school youths, women and indigenous communities through non-formal education, bilingual literacy programs and multilingual learning, Wang said. "They are living examples of Confucius' idea of education for all," he said. Spiritual pursuits Lin Wu, secretary of the Shandong Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China, said that Confucian thought took root in China and reflects the spiritual pursuits of the Chinese nation, embodying the distinctive charm of Chinese civilization. He said that the emphasis of Confucian thought on benevolence and harmony in diversity, as well as The Doctrine of the Mean, could offer important inspiration for addressing global challenges and problems facing humanity today. "As the world changes rapidly, people expect to meet through culture," Lin said, describing the festival as a platform for cultural exchange and mutual learning. He also emphasized the importance of preserving cultural diversity and ensuring that traditional culture remains connected to contemporary life. In a video address to the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations, which this year focuses on "Civilization, Order and Justice", Thomas Bach, ninth president and honorary president for life of the International Olympic Committee, drew a connection between Confucian thought and the values of the Olympic movement. Bach recalled his visit to Qufu several years ago, saying that it gave him an opportunity to see firsthand the common ground between Confucian thought and the Olympic ideal. Confucius recognized the importance of cultivating both body and mind, Bach said, an idea that also finds an echo in the ancient Roman maxim about "a sound mind in a sound body". He welcomed the forum's efforts to explore connections between civilizations and cultures, saying that dialogue has become increasingly important in a divided world, and called for a shared spirit of understanding and peaceful coexistence. Suos Yara, chairman of the Commission on Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Information of the National Assembly of Cambodia, said that the forum's theme was particularly relevant to a world facing rapid technological changes, growing interdependence and a series of interconnected challenges. He said that civilization gives people a sense of identity and wisdom, while order creates the conditions for peaceful coexistence and justice helps sustain that order. The Nishan forum provides an opportunity to draw on different civilizational experiences and perspectives in addressing challenges that no country can tackle alone, he said. The contemporary value of Confucianism, global governance, artificial intelligence and other issues concerning humanity's future are among the topics being discussed.

item.title: Mid-Autumn surge sets stage for National Day travel
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-29
China's three-day Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, which ended on Sunday, served as a prelude to the upcoming weeklong National Day holiday starting on Thursday, with travel agencies and industry insiders reporting robust bookings across both breaks. Some people have combined the two holidays by taking several days of leave in between, creating what they called the "longest consecutive break of the year" — a stretch of up to 13 days that has fueled demand for both short — and long-haul trips. Symbolizing harvests and family reunions, Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth month of the traditional Chinese calendar. Traditions such as enjoying the full moon and eating mooncakes have driven strong demand for destinations with a rich traditional Chinese atmosphere. Online travel agency Qunar said that flight bookings to domestic destinations had surged more than 60 percent year-on-year on Friday, calling the holiday the "most booming" Mid-Autumn Festival break in recent years. Night-tour bookings on its platform more than doubled compared with the same period last year. Nanjing in Jiangsu province and Hangzhou in Zhejiang province were top choices for night tours to appreciate the full moon from a boat on Nanjing's Qinhuai River or on Hangzhou's West Lake. Wang Luying, 28, a Shanghai resident who spent the holiday in Hangzhou with her boyfriend, said that despite sweltering weather and large crowds, they walked along the West Lake and looked up at the moon as illuminated boats floated on the water. "It was poetically beautiful," she said. Demand has also grown for travel related to appreciating the autumn scenery, with travelers seeking out forests and grasslands, as well as ancient villages. Travel portal Tuniu reported surging visitor numbers to Huangshan in Anhui province, Shangrao in Jiangxi province, which is known for its well-preserved ancient villages and harvest views, and Altay in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, famed for its mountain and grassland scenery. Outbound travel has also benefited from the extended break, with many people opting to take longer overseas trips. Qunar said that as of Sunday, the final day of the Mid-Autumn break, more than 20 percent of passengers who had booked departing flights on its platform had yet to book return tickets — a sign that many were still extending their trips. London and Los Angeles joined Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Seoul, Istanbul and Sydney among the top 10 overseas destinations for the holiday. "The idea of extending the break to 13 days has greatly sparked people's passion for travel, so we've seen both short-distance and long-distance tours surge, especially trips to places that require long traveling hours," said Qi Chunguang, vice-president of Tuniu. He added that the popularity of tours to appreciate the autumn scenery at destinations rich in Chinese culture is expected to continue rising next week.

item.title: Hi Five China: Huaihua's bamboo breakthrough
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-28
Hi Five China: Huaihua's bamboo breakthrough In Huaihua, a mountain city in Central China, you might be surprised by what bamboo can do. Keyboards, mice and even truck bed panels can all be made from bamboo. Huaihua is home to more than 112,000 hectares of bamboo forest and some 310 million bamboo plants. For at least 7,000 years, people here have lived and worked with bamboo. Today, that long tradition is taking on new possibilities. In 2025, "bamboo as a substitute for plastic" was included in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, which calls for accelerating the development of bamboo-based alternatives to plastic. Huaihua is already putting that idea into practice. Its bamboo truck bed panels have entered the supply chains of international automakers, including Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, offering an alternative to steel. Through the Huaihua International Land Port, bamboo products reach more than 50 countries and regions. Follow China Daily reporter Yan An on the ground to see how a piece of bamboo makes its way from the mountains to the world — and how China's green development is creating benefits beyond its borders.
